title: Why Children Say 'Goed'
paragraphs: Among the most reliably observed curiosities of language acquisition is the course by which English-speaking children learn the past tense of irregular verbs. A child of two will typically say went and came correctly. Some months later the same child begins to produce goed and comed, and may do so intermittently for years before the correct forms return for good. The pattern is described as U-shaped: performance declines after an early peak and recovers later. Because the child has evidently not forgotten went, which continues to appear alongside goed, the decline cannot be a simple loss of knowledge, and what it is instead has become a test case for competing views of how linguistic knowledge is represented.

On the account defended by Silvia Marchetti, the child's grammar contains two distinct mechanisms. Irregular forms are stored in memory and retrieved as wholes; regular forms are generated by a rule that appends a suffix to the stem. The early went reflects retrieval from memory of a form the child has heard often. The later goed appears when the child has acquired the rule and, on a given occasion, fails to retrieve the stored form quickly enough to block it. Overregularization is thus the sound of a rule filling a gap left by a lapse of memory, and it should be rarer for verbs the child hears frequently, since their stored forms are more readily retrieved.

Owen Dunmore and his collaborators reject the division. Their models consist of a single associative network trained on pairs of stems and past forms, with no component that could be called a rule. Such networks, they report, pass through a stage of producing goed-like forms as the proportion of regular verbs in their training input rises, and they too produce fewer errors for frequent irregulars, since frequent pairs are more strongly represented. What Marchetti attributes to the interaction of two mechanisms, Dunmore attributes to the statistics of one. The appeal of the account lies in its economy, and in its refusal to posit a rule that no one has observed directly.

The evidence, in my judgment, favors Marchetti, though less decisively than her proponents claim. Children overregularize only a small fraction of the time, perhaps one irregular in twenty-five, a rate the dual-mechanism account predicts from occasional retrieval failure and the networks reproduce only when their training schedules are adjusted after the fact. More telling, children almost never make the reverse error of giving a regular verb an irregular past, as a purely associative system attracted by similar-sounding neighbors should sometimes do. Yet it would be premature to treat the matter as closed. Much of the disagreement turns on what is to count as a rule, and a network that behaved in every respect as though it contained one might reasonably be said to do so.

viewpoints.position: Two mechanisms, memorized irregulars and a suffixing rule; overregularization is the rule filling a retrieval lapse.
A single associative network with no rule reproduces the U-shaped pattern from input statistics alone.
Error rates and the asymmetry of errors favor Marchetti, but the dispute may be partly about what counts as a rule.

lowResSummary: Author weighs dual-mechanism and network accounts of children's overregularization, favors the former on error patterns, and doubts the dispute is settled.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.A: The U-shaped learning of irregular past tenses is better explained by a rule-plus-memory account than by a single network, though the question is not fully settled.
choices.B: Children's overregularization errors demonstrate that the rules of a grammar cannot be observed directly but only inferred from the errors children make.
choices.C: Because connectionist networks reproduce the frequency effects seen in children's errors, the dual-mechanism account offers no genuine explanatory advantage over them.
choices.D: Children's performance on irregular verbs declines after an early peak because they temporarily forget forms that they had previously learned correctly.
choices.E: The debate between Marchetti and Dunmore is merely verbal, since it turns entirely on how the word 'rule' is to be defined.

explanations.A: Correct. Paragraph 4: 'The evidence, in my judgment, favors Marchetti, though less decisively than her proponents claim... it would be premature to treat the matter as closed.'
explanations.B: Wrong part. Unobservability of rules is Dunmore's selling point, not the passage's conclusion.
explanations.C: Opposite. The author grants the frequency point but finds the error rate and the asymmetry of errors 'more telling' for Marchetti.
explanations.D: Opposite. Paragraph 1 rules this out: 'the child has evidently not forgotten went.'
explanations.E: Extreme. The author says 'much of the disagreement' is definitional, not that it is 'merely verbal' or turns 'entirely' on a definition.

questions.keyTakeaway: A verdict with a hedge ('favors... though less decisively') must appear in the main point with the hedge intact.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Marchetti's account predicts that overregularization errors should be

choices.A: more common for regular verbs than for irregular verbs
choices.B: most frequent at the earliest stage of language acquisition
choices.C: confined to irregular verbs whose stems resemble those of regular verbs
choices.D: equally likely for all irregular verbs once the child has acquired the rule
choices.E: less frequent for irregular verbs that the child hears often

explanations.A: Shell game. Overregularization by definition applies a regular pattern to irregular verbs; regular verbs cannot be overregularized.
explanations.B: Opposite. The earliest stage is the correct went; errors appear only after the rule is acquired.
explanations.C: Wrong part. Similarity-based attraction is a feature of associative networks, which the author mentions in paragraph 4, not of Marchetti's account.
explanations.D: Opposite. The account predicts frequency-sensitivity, not equal likelihood.
explanations.E: Correct. 'It should be rarer for verbs the child hears frequently, since their stored forms are more readily retrieved.'

questions.keyTakeaway: Marchetti's paragraph ends with its one prediction; detail questions about a theory's predictions go to that sentence.

questions.stem: The author mentions that children almost never give a regular verb an irregular past primarily in order to

choices.A: show that children acquire regular verbs before they acquire irregular ones
choices.B: concede a point in favor of Dunmore's associative models of acquisition
choices.C: cite an asymmetry that a purely associative account would not lead one to expect
choices.D: explain why overregularization errors occur only about one time in twenty-five
choices.E: illustrate the kind of error that Marchetti's rule would produce if retrieval failed

explanations.A: Out of scope. The order of acquisition of verb classes is never discussed.
explanations.B: Opposite. The sentence is introduced as 'more telling' evidence against the associative account.
explanations.C: Correct. A system 'attracted by similar-sounding neighbors should sometimes' make the reverse error, and children do not.
explanations.D: Shell game. The rate and the asymmetry are two separate pieces of evidence; one does not explain the other.
explanations.E: Wrong part. Marchetti's rule produces goed, the forward error, not irregularized regulars.

questions.keyTakeaway: 'More telling' introduces the author's strongest evidence; its function is to discriminate between the two theories.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Dunmore's models can most accurately be described as

choices.A: dismissive of their relevance to the acquisition of irregular verbs
choices.B: convinced that they will eventually supersede the dual-mechanism account
choices.C: critical of their reliance on training input that children never actually receive
choices.D: skeptical of their adequacy while acknowledging the appeal of their parsimony
choices.E: persuaded that they already contain a rule in all but name

explanations.A: Extreme. The author engages the models in detail and treats them as a live alternative.
explanations.B: Opposite. The author judges that the evidence 'favors Marchetti.'
explanations.C: Out of scope. The author criticizes adjusted 'training schedules,' not the content of the input.
explanations.D: Correct. 'The appeal of the account lies in its economy' is granted; the evidence nonetheless 'favors Marchetti.'
explanations.E: Wrong force. The author says such a network 'might reasonably be said' to contain a rule, a conditional, not a settled conviction.

questions.keyTakeaway: Attitude answers must match the author's hedges: 'appeal... economy' plus 'favors Marchetti' equals skeptical but fair.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following?

choices.A: The more economical of two competing accounts should be accepted unless it is directly contradicted by the evidence.
choices.B: Whether a system contains a rule may be settled by how it behaves rather than by inspecting its components.
choices.C: The dual-mechanism account will be confirmed once a rule has been observed directly in the child's grammar.
choices.D: Children who overregularize have not yet stored the irregular forms of the verbs in question in memory.
choices.E: Associative networks cannot reproduce the frequency effects observed in children's overregularization errors.

explanations.A: Out of scope. The author notes economy as an appeal but never adopts a rule for choosing between theories on that basis.
explanations.B: Correct. The final sentence: 'a network that behaved in every respect as though it contained one might reasonably be said to do so.'
explanations.C: Extreme. The author does not make confirmation depend on direct observation; Dunmore's point about unobservability is reported, not endorsed as a standard.
explanations.D: Opposite. Paragraph 1 says the child 'has evidently not forgotten went'; the forms are stored but not always retrieved.
explanations.E: Opposite. Paragraph 3 reports that the networks 'too produce fewer errors for frequent irregulars.'

questions.keyTakeaway: The last sentence quietly commits the author to a behavioral criterion for rules; the correct answer abstracts that commitment.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.A: A phenomenon is described; an explanation is proposed and then rejected in favor of a second explanation.
choices.B: Two explanations of a phenomenon are presented, and the author shows that they are ultimately compatible.
choices.C: A phenomenon is described, and the author proposes an original explanation that supersedes two earlier ones.
choices.D: A phenomenon is described; two competing explanations are presented; the author favors one while noting that the dispute may be partly definitional.
choices.E: A phenomenon is described, and evidence is presented showing that neither of the existing explanations can account for its most important and well-documented features.

explanations.A: Opposite. The first explanation (Marchetti's) is the one the author favors, not the one rejected.
explanations.B: Opposite. The author favors one; he does not reconcile them, though he notes a definitional blur.
explanations.C: Out of scope. The author offers no third explanation.
explanations.D: Correct. Paragraphs 1 through 4 follow exactly this sequence, ending with 'much of the disagreement turns on what is to count as a rule.'
explanations.E: Extreme. The author says the evidence 'favors Marchetti.'

questions.keyTakeaway: Organization answers must get the order of views and the author's final stance right; the hedge about definitions is part of the structure.
